blocks.text: Stereoisomers are of two types: optical isomers and cis-trans isomers (next topic). Optical isomers have identical physical and chemical properties except their ability to rotate plane-polarised light. Such isomers are optically active, and the rotation of the plane of polarisation is optical activity. If a compound rotates the plane to the right (clockwise) it is dextrorotatory, shown (+); if to the left (anticlockwise), laevorotatory, shown (-).

blocks.title: Keep in mind: the polarimeter
blocks.text: A polarimeter detects and measures optical activity. Monochromatic light (one wavelength) is passed through a polariser so that it vibrates in one plane, then through a solution of the compound. If the plane is rotated, the compound is optically active; if not, it is optically inactive.

blocks.alt: Unpolarised light, with vibrations in all directions, passes a polariser and becomes plane-polarised light vibrating in one plane. It passes through a sample solution and comes out turned either to the right (dextrorotatory, +) or to the left (laevorotatory, -).
blocks.caption: Optical rotation of plane-polarised light (original diagram after Figure 19.4).
blocks.long_description: Ordinary light vibrates in every direction at right angles to its path. A polariser lets through only the vibrations in one plane. An optically active substance turns that plane through an angle; one enantiomer turns it to the right and the other by the same angle to the left.

blocks.text: The basic requirement for optical activity is that the molecule is non-superimposable on its mirror image. Our left and right hands are the everyday example: they are mirror images, but one cannot be placed exactly on the other. Molecules that can be superimposed on their mirror images are achiral and optically inactive.

blocks.alt: A left hand seen from the palm side, a vertical mirror, and a right hand that is its mirror image. On the right, the two hands are placed one on the other with the palms facing the same way: the thumbs point in opposite directions, so the hands cannot be superimposed.
blocks.caption: Left and right hands are mirror images that cannot be superimposed (original diagram after Figure 19.5).
blocks.long_description: An object that cannot be superimposed on its mirror image is chiral, from the Greek word for hand. A molecule with one carbon atom bonded to four different groups is chiral in the same way, and its two mirror-image forms are enantiomers.

blocks.title: Chiral carbon
blocks.text: A chiral (asymmetric) carbon is a carbon atom bonded to four different atoms or groups. A molecule with only one chiral carbon is always chiral and optically active; a molecule with more than one may or may not be.

Lactic acid, CH3-CH(OH)-COOH, has one chiral carbon bonded to CH3, H, OH and COOH. In three dimensions it exists as two stereoisomers that are non-superimposable mirror images: enantiomers (from the Greek enantio, opposite). Enantiomers have identical physical and chemical properties but rotate plane-polarised light by the same amount in opposite directions, and they can act differently in living systems. A 50:50 mixture of the (+) and (-) forms is optically inactive; it is a racemic mixture, written with (+/-) before the name. So lactic acid exists as (+)-lactic acid, (-)-lactic acid and the inactive racemic mixture.

Stereoisomers that contain at least two similar chiral carbons and also have a plane of symmetry are optically inactive. The plane divides the molecule into two halves that are mirror images of each other; each half would rotate the plane of polarised light in the opposite direction, so the rotations cancel inside the molecule (internal compensation). Such stereoisomers are meso forms; meso-tartaric acid is the classic example.

blocks.alt: Left: two wedge-and-dash drawings of lactic acid on either side of a mirror line, each with a starred chiral carbon bearing CH3, COOH, H and OH; one is the mirror image of the other. Right: meso-tartaric acid as COOH, H-C-OH, H-C-OH, COOH with a dashed plane of symmetry between the two chiral carbons.
blocks.caption: The enantiomers of lactic acid and meso-tartaric acid (original diagram after the book's structures).
blocks.long_description: The two forms of lactic acid have the same four groups round the chiral carbon, but in mirror-image arrangements that cannot be superimposed. Meso-tartaric acid has two chiral carbons, but its top half is the mirror image of its bottom half, so the molecule as a whole is not chiral and does not rotate plane-polarised light.

blocks.title: How many optical isomers?
blocks.text: The maximum number of optical isomers is 2^n, where n is the number of chiral carbon atoms. The number is smaller if two or more chiral carbons are similar.
